source.title: Standard Treatment Workflow (STW) for the Management of Epistaxis
source.publisher: Department of Health Research, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India

condition_description: Epistaxis means bleeding from the nose. Most nosebleeds in adults are minor and related to dry air, nose picking, trauma, or uncontrolled blood pressure. Most can be managed at home with simple first aid.

sections.label: Red Flag Signs: Go to Hospital
items: Nosebleed that does not stop after 20 minutes of correct first aid
Nosebleed with very heavy or rapid blood loss causing dizziness, weakness, or faintness
Nosebleed only from one side of the nose persistently, without a clear cause like trauma, this may need investigation
Nosebleed with nasal blockage, a visible mass, or changes in vision or the eye, could indicate a serious nasal or sinus condition
Nosebleed in a person on blood thinners or with a known bleeding disorder
Nosebleed in a person with uncontrolled high blood pressure
Nosebleed in a person after head trauma
Nosebleed with bleeding from other sites at the same time, gums, skin bruising, blood in urine or stool, may indicate a blood disorder
Recurrent, profuse nosebleeds in a teenage boy, requires specialist evaluation

sections.label: First Aid for Nosebleed at Home
items: Sit upright and lean slightly forward, do not tilt the head back, as this causes blood to flow down the throat and may cause vomiting or choking
Breathe through your mouth
Pinch the soft part of the nose (just below the bony bridge) firmly with your thumb and index finger, this is called Trotter's position
Hold the nose pinched continuously for 10 minutes without releasing, use a clock to time it, as most people underestimate the time
Apply a cold compress or ice wrapped in a cloth to the nose and cheeks
After 10 minutes, gently release and check if bleeding has stopped
If bleeding continues, repeat the pinching for another 10 minutes
Avoid blowing the nose forcefully immediately after the bleeding stops
Avoid hot drinks, physical exertion, and bending over for several hours after a nosebleed
Apply a small amount of petroleum jelly or liquid paraffin inside the nostril daily if you get recurrent nosebleeds due to dry air, this helps keep the mucosa moist
Most nosebleeds in children are from the front of the nose (Little's area) due to dry air or nose picking and stop quickly with simple pressure

sections.label: See a Doctor
items: Nosebleed that stopped but recurs frequently
Known high blood pressure with recurring nosebleeds, blood pressure needs to be checked and controlled
Nosebleed in a person with diabetes
Nosebleed in a child that keeps coming back despite no obvious cause

sections.label: Go to Hospital Without Delay
items: Nosebleed not stopping after 20 minutes of sustained pressure
Heavy blood loss with dizziness, weakness, or rapid pulse
Nosebleed following a head injury
Nosebleed with associated bleeding from other sites
Nosebleed with one-sided nasal blockage, vision changes, or a visible swelling in the nose or face

review.notes: All nasal packing, cauterization, drug, and surgical steps excluded. First aid pinching technique retained as it is a non-drug emergency response step sourced directly from the document and essential for safe home management.
